passages.text: Aksum linked the northern Ethiopian highlands to the Red Sea through Adulis. Its monuments and inscriptions reveal a kingdom connected to African and Mediterranean exchange networks. The city also retained religious and ceremonial importance after its political power diminished.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Stoneworkers carved enormous stelae from single blocks. Some imitate multi-storey buildings, preserving an architectural vocabulary in stone.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The carved stelae belong especially to the third and fourth centuries CE. Royal tombs and later palace ruins reveal several phases of monumental construction.

passages.title: Writing and ideas
passages.text: King Ezana's fourth-century inscriptions used Greek, Sabaean and Ge'ez. Their multiple languages make connections across the region visible.

passages.title: Writing and ideas
passages.text: Christianity was introduced during the fourth century. Church building subsequently became part of the city's sacred landscape.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Adulis connected maritime commerce with inland routes, while ivory trade linked Aksum with Sudan.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Later Ethiopian emperors continued to be crowned at Aksum. Political decline did not erase its ceremonial role.

passages.text: The Almohads made Marrakesh a center of government and learning while maintaining a major Iberian center at Seville. Monumental mosques, gates and city walls gave their rule an enduring architectural presence.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Kutubiyya mosque and minaret formed a major landmark in Marrakesh. Walls and monumental gateways also shaped the imperial capital.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Almohad decoration emphasized organized geometric patterns and increasingly schematic ornament.

passages.title: Ideas and learning
passages.text: The courts at Marrakesh and Seville supported Islamic learning within a program of religious reform.

passages.title: Urban life
passages.text: Fez expanded under the Almohads, with the old city reaching the extent described by UNESCO as its present-day size.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Almohad Marrakesh remained a capital into the thirteenth century. Later dynasties inherited a city whose monuments continued to structure urban life.

passages.text: The Almoravids governed from Marrakesh and connected Saharan routes with North African and Iberian towns. Their rule supported major religious buildings and crafts, while their capital helped shape the urban geography of the western Islamic world.

passages.title: Technology and towns
passages.text: Marrakesh was an Almoravid foundation. Its palm grove is traditionally attributed to their period, linking the capital with a managed cultivated landscape.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Ali ibn Yusuf commissioned a richly worked mosque minbar in 1137. It later became associated with the Kutubiyya Mosque.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Textile manufacture in Almeria shows that Almoravid cultural production included luxurious fabrics as well as mosque building.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Almoravid power connected important ports with trans-Saharan commerce. The state's economy crossed both sea and desert.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Almohads replaced Almoravid rule in Marrakesh in the mid-twelfth century and retained the city as a capital.

passages.text: Asante architecture joined construction skill with visual language and religious practice. Surviving shrine buildings near Kumasi preserve parts of a tradition that remained meaningful beyond the period of imperial power.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders arranged timber and bamboo structures around courtyards, applying mud plaster to walls and originally roofing them with thatch.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wall reliefs combine spirals with animal, bird and plant forms. Motifs related to Adinkra convey meanings as well as decorate surfaces.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shrines are places for consultation with deities before important decisions. Their symbolic features belong to continuing religious practice.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Maintaining earthen buildings requires responding to heavy rain, humidity and damage to organic materials. Architectural survival depends on repeated care.

passages.text: Tenochtitlan brought canals, markets, workshops and ceremonial architecture into a large lake city. This card focuses on the capital's civic and artistic life within the Aztec imperial world.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Canals and raised causeways connected the capital to surrounding lakeshore towns. Canoes carried people and goods through the urban network.

passages.title: Water and daily life
passages.text: Aqueducts supplied fresh water, while neighborhood communities maintained local temples and markets.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Stone carvers used stone and hardwood tools, fiber cords, water and sand to shape even hard materials into detailed sculpture.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: The Templo Mayor paired shrines to Tlaloc and Huitzilopochtli. Successive rulers enlarged the complex, sometimes also responding to flooding and unstable ground.

passages.title: Craft and exchange
passages.text: The capital's markets offered food and luxury goods. Its neighborhoods included potters, weavers, sculptors, lapidaries and featherworkers.
Tenochtitlan fell in 1521. Spanish rulers built a new colonial capital over the devastated city.

passages.text: Benin's court commissioned brass sculpture to preserve royal memory and express authority. This Edo kingdom was centered in present-day Nigeria, distinct from the modern country named Benin.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: An incoming oba commissioned a commemorative head honoring his predecessor. These idealized royal images emphasize kingship rather than individual facial likeness.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Brass-casting guild artists produced rectangular plaques for the palace. A surviving example is dated approximately 1540 to 1570.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Palace courtyards and galleries included wooden pillars covered with cast brass plaques.

passages.title: Historical memory
passages.text: Scholars interpret palace plaques as an archive later consulted about court ritual and regalia.

passages.title: Historical evidence
passages.text: British removal of royal works in 1897 disrupted their original contexts. Scholars therefore combine stylistic and material evidence when reconstructing their chronology.

passages.text: Carolingian rulers made learning, Christian worship and patronage part of imperial government. Their workshops and scholars adapted older traditions into books, buildings and objects that influenced medieval Europe.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: The drive for accurate, readable texts encouraged Carolingian minuscule, a clear script based on Roman letter forms.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: Charlemagne gathered scholars including Alcuin, Theodulf and Paul the Lombard. Court patronage supported educational and liturgical reform.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Illuminated books and carved ivory panels combined classical figures with local ornamental traditions. Precious bindings could include gems and pearls.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: The palace chapel at Aachen has an octagonal core, an encircling aisle, upper galleries and a dome. Its antique columns were probably brought from Rome and Ravenna.

passages.title: Ideas and institutions
passages.text: Charlemagne received the imperial crown in Rome in 800. The ceremony tied royal authority to a Christian interpretation of Roman imperial tradition.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Carolingian art continued after Charlemagne's death and political fragmentation. The end of a unified realm did not end its workshops or manuscript traditions.

passages.text: Carthage grew on the Gulf of Tunis into a major center of Punic civilization and Mediterranean commerce. Its ports connected communities, goods and artistic traditions. This card concerns the Punic city and its power before Roman destruction, rather than the later Roman city built on the same site.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The surviving Punic harbor remains make maritime infrastructure central to understanding Carthage's commercial power.

passages.title: Arts and beliefs
passages.text: Stelae from the sacred tophet show varied cultural influences. The imagery is evidence of artistic exchange as well as religious practice.

passages.title: Knowledge
passages.text: Magon was remembered as an agronomist and Hannon as a navigator. Agriculture and seafaring both belonged to Carthage's intellectual legacy.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Later Roman buildings at Carthage belong to a refounded city. They should not be attributed automatically to Punic builders.
Rome destroyed Punic Carthage in 146 BCE. A Roman city was later established on the site.

passages.text: The Chimu kingdom made Chan Chan a major center on Peru's north coast. Its earthen compounds, craft production and water systems show how a large city organized resources in a dry coastal environment.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Canals and irrigation supported agriculture around Chan Chan. Roads helped connect the kingdom along the northern coast.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Large walled compounds contained open courts, temples, dwellings, storage spaces, reservoirs and funerary platforms.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Earthen walls carried relief decoration with abstract patterns and human or animal subjects.

passages.title: Craft and work
passages.text: Specialized production areas supported weaving, woodworking and metalworking. These activities were part of the city's planned fabric.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Storage and water-management installations supported the city alongside agricultural land beyond its monumental center.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: The kingdom reached its height in the fifteenth century before incorporation into the Inca Empire. The source used here does not establish a precise conquest year.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Polychrome reliefs gave palace walls a visual language of royal history and symbolism.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Outer, inner and private courtyards structured access through each palace, making social distinctions part of the built environment.

passages.title: Continuity

passages.text: Twentieth-century Copenhagen became a meeting place for physicists working on quantum theory. This focused chapter follows the institute, discussions and everyday arrangements that helped international collaboration take root.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Bohr's Institute for Theoretical Physics was dedicated in Copenhagen in March 1921, after fundraising and approval of the project.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: During the 1920s, visiting researchers exchanged ideas in Copenhagen. Discussions could happen in small groups and at dinners with the Bohr family.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: In 1927, Bohr presented complementarity: different experimental arrangements can require different, mutually exclusive descriptions of a quantum phenomenon. The proposal became a focus of debate.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the 1930s, a new mathematics institute was built beside the physics institute. Shared classrooms and a canteen were intended to support closer collaboration.

passages.text: This chapter follows sixteenth-century Denmark-Norway through astronomy, printing and royal architecture. Tycho Brahe's observatory shows how scientific work depended on buildings, instruments and supporting crafts.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Under Danish royal patronage, Tycho Brahe built Uraniborg on Hven between 1576 and 1580. The island is now Swedish but was then Danish.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Uraniborg included a printing office and a water mill for making paper. Publishing and material production supported the observatory's work.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Tycho established Stjerneborg in 1584. Sheltered instrument spaces reduced exposure to wind and helped stabilize observations.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Frederik II began rebuilding Kronborg as a Renaissance castle in 1574. Its courtyard, carved sandstone and decorated chapel formed a major royal setting.

passages.text: Ancient Egypt brought together royal power, skilled workshops and a durable written culture along the Nile. Its art changed substantially across the Old and Middle Kingdoms. Pyramids, family memorials and ordinary letters reveal different parts of that society; surviving evidence is often weighted toward elite tombs.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: At Saqqara, Djoser's Step Pyramid formed the center of a complex of stone buildings and underground chambers. Later builders developed smooth-sided pyramids.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Papyrus sheets were made by layering strips of the stalk's inner pith and drying them under pressure. Sheets could be joined into writing rolls.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Old Kingdom tomb chapels depicted food offerings and agricultural work. These images were meant to sustain the dead, so they are more than documentary pictures of daily life.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Middle Kingdom jewelers placed tiny inlays on ornaments and sometimes decorated their backs with elaborate chasing, visible principally to their wearers.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Unis had religious spells carved inside his pyramid late in Dynasty 5. Later kings, and eventually queens, also received these Pyramid Texts.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Middle Kingdom memorials increasingly pictured extended families and associates. Such monuments show religious commemoration reaching beyond the ruler alone.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Papyrus carried accounts, letters and legal agreements as well as religious works. Black ink usually supplied the main text; red ink could mark emphasis.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The same marsh plant also supplied material for baskets, sandals, ropes and small boats. A writing technology belonged to a much wider craft economy.

passages.text: The medieval Soninke empire of Ghana prospered through trans-Saharan exchange. Its power rested on commercial connections and political centers such as Kumbi Saleh, rather than a fixed border enclosing one people.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Gold moved north while salt moved south. Taxing imports and exports helped support imperial rule.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Camel caravans made long desert journeys possible; traders connected different ecological regions rather than transporting goods within a single uniform landscape.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Savanna agriculture and livestock breeding supported the societies through which the trade routes passed.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Al-Bakri described gold-adorned court equipment and clothing. Such written testimony records royal display, not the possessions of every household.

passages.title: Political change
passages.text: By the late twelfth century Ghana had lost its dominant position in the western Sudan gold trade as routes shifted. Its decline was a process, not a securely dated disappearance of Soninke society.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Royal Society's first meeting followed Christopher Wren's astronomy lecture in London in 1660. Its members gathered observations, performed experiments and discussed results.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Henry Oldenburg began Philosophical Transactions in 1665. The same year, Robert Hooke published the close observations collected in Micrographia.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The early Royal Society drew members from professional and aristocratic circles and admitted only men. Its meeting rooms represented a restricted part of society.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The English and Scottish Acts of Union created Great Britain on 1 May 1707. The new parliament first met that October.

passages.text: The Etruscans lived in a network of central Italian city-states. Metalworking, imported luxury materials and distinctive funerary art reveal communities deeply involved in Mediterranean exchange.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Bucchero pottery has a glossy black surface and often uses shapes associated with metal vessels.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze workers made decorated chariots, vessels, mirrors and sculpture. Access to copper and iron supported their craft traditions.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Greek painted pottery was highly valued in Etruria. Trade also brought ivory, amber and other materials used by local artists.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: At Cerveteri, rock-cut tombs reproduce features of houses. Their arrangement into streets and small squares offers clues to settlement planning.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Painted tombs at Tarquinia preserve scenes of living, dying and religious belief. Funerary images provide evidence that short surviving inscriptions often cannot supply.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Roman expansion absorbed the Etruscan cities over time. Their culture did not end on the map's current 323 BCE snapshot boundary.

passages.text: The Canal du Midi project used locks, aqueducts, bridges, spillways and tunnels to make an inland water route. UNESCO dates the wider historic works to 1667 through 1694.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The canal's water-supply system drew on the Montagne Noire. The Saint-Ferreol dam was a major engineering component.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: After 1661, Louis XIV enlarged Versailles through work directed first by Le Vau and later by Jules Hardouin-Mansart. Its architecture developed across successive campaigns.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Andre Le Notre organized Versailles' gardens with long axes, planted beds, hedges, water and fountains. The landscape formed part of the royal residence's design.

passages.text: Frankish communities expressed wealth and identity through dress and skilled metalwork. The map's Frankish Kingdom record covers only part of a longer history and should not imply that Frankish culture began in 600.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Women wore belted tunics with a wrap or cloak. Pendants hung from belts, and jewelry included earrings, necklaces and hairpins.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Small paired brooches were common in earlier centuries; large single disk brooches became fashionable in the 600s.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A mid-seventh-century disk brooch combines gold with garnet, colored glass and mother-of-pearl. Small fastening objects could display elaborate material contrasts.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Charlemagne became king of the Franks in 768 and emperor in 800. Imperial culture grew from earlier Frankish traditions of patronage and fine metalwork.

passages.text: In late-sixteenth- and early-seventeenth-century Genoa, mercantile wealth reshaped streets, houses and hospitality. The Rolli palaces reveal how private residences served the republic's public business.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, Genoa developed the Strade Nuove as a coordinated district of streets and aristocratic palaces above the older city.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The palaces adapted to steep and confined sites with open staircases, courtyards and garden-facing loggias. Frescoes and stucco decorated their interiors.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The Senate established the Rolli list of private palaces used to lodge distinguished official visitors. Hosting state guests became an obligation attached to selected elite homes.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Rolli system sorted residences into categories corresponding to different ranks of guest. Hospitality made social hierarchy part of the organization of official visits.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Architectural treatises spread knowledge of Genoa's new streets and palaces beyond the city in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

passages.text: Great Zimbabwe was a stone-built center created by ancestors of the Shona. Its surviving walls preserve part of a larger settlement of homes, courtyards and monumental enclosures.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders fitted local granite slabs together without mortar. Successive courses stepped inward, giving the curving walls a stabilizing inward slope.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Eight surviving soapstone bird sculptures combine human and bird features. Their precise meaning remains uncertain; an association with royal authority is one interpretation.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Stone walls stood beside homes made from daga, a building material of earth, with thatched roofs. Painted surfaces and enclosed courtyards formed parts of the lived settlement.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Excavations recovered imported glass beads, ceramics from China and Persia, and coins from Kilwa. These objects place the inland settlement within long-distance exchange networks; they do not, by themselves, identify every trader or route.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Six soapstone birds came from the Hill Complex's Eastern Enclosure. Their setting supports interpretations involving ritual or royal authority, but their original arrangement and precise meaning remain uncertain.

Great Zimbabwe did not simply empty in 1450. A study combining radiocarbon dates, stratigraphy and imported objects places occupation at least into the sixteenth century and probably the seventeenth, after its main building peak in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. The chronology does not identify a single conquest or establish one cause for the loss of political prominence. The site remains a place of spiritual practice for contemporary communities; the decline of a capital did not mean the disappearance of its people.

passages.text: The Greek city-states formed a varied political and cultural world. These examples focus on Athens and Classical sculpture; Athenian institutions should not be assumed to describe every Greek community.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Athenian potters controlled the air admitted to a kiln in successive firing stages to produce contrasting black and red surfaces.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Red-figure vase painting developed around 530 BCE. Brush-drawn details gave painters greater freedom to show anatomy, fabric and movement.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Polykleitos developed a system of bodily proportions. Many renowned Greek bronze compositions are known through later marble copies and written descriptions.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: The marble Parthenon belonged to the building program associated with Perikles and the worship of Athena on the Athenian Acropolis.

passages.title: Ideas and institutions
passages.text: In Classical Athens, adult male citizens participated in the assembly. This was a particular civic institution, not political participation for every resident.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Different vessel shapes served storage, water carrying, drinking and ritual. Pottery images complement written evidence about Athenian life.

passages.text: Gunditjmara people maintain a living relationship with Country in south-western Victoria. At Budj Bim, generations shaped waterways into an aquaculture landscape. The map's imported date range describes its snapshots, not the beginning or end of Gunditjmara society.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders used volcanic stone to redirect water through channels, weirs and dams. These connected structures trapped, held and harvested kooyang, the short-finned eel.

passages.title: Science and environment
passages.text: Aquaculture depended on knowledge of seasonal eel movement, water flow and wetland ecology. Water management and food production were linked practices.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Kurtonitj preserves stone house sites alongside eel traps, channels and trees used for smoking eels. Settlement and food processing belong in the same landscape.

passages.title: Arts and knowledge
passages.text: Storytelling, dance and basket weaving transmit knowledge across generations. Fibre baskets also belong to the practical technology of eel harvesting.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: A cultural weir restored traditional flows into Tae Rak after earlier drainage. Gunditjmara customary responsibilities and cultural connections continue today.

passages.text: Under Hafsid rule, Tunis was a wealthy center of the western Islamic world. Its urban history joins markets, religious institutions and residential neighborhoods. The surviving medina contains work from several dynasties, so individual buildings require their own dates and patronage histories.

passages.title: Technology and towns
passages.text: Northern and southern suburbs developed in the thirteenth century around the older central medina. Tunis was an expanding urban settlement, not only a palace city.

passages.title: Arts and exchange
passages.text: Tunis connected the Maghreb, southern Europe and lands to the east. These links encouraged exchanges in architecture and the arts.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Souqs, residential quarters and gates formed an interconnected townscape. Their survival helps historians study urban organization alongside individual monuments.

passages.title: Learning and beliefs
passages.text: Mosques and madrasas belonged to the city's institutional landscape. Surviving examples span both the Hafsid era and later periods.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Subsequent rulers added new palaces, residences and religious buildings. The medina records continuity and change across political transitions.

passages.text: The Han ruled China for four centuries, with a brief interruption, and set the pattern that later dynasties followed: an emperor advised by scholar-officials trained in the Confucian classics, a census-taking bureaucracy, and a capital laid out on a grid. Paper, the seismoscope and the first great history of China were made under the Han, and the Silk Road opened during their reign. The Chinese still call their majority people the Han.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Cai Lun presents the court with paper made from bark, hemp and rags. Paper travels west along the Silk Road and reaches Europe a thousand years later.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Zhang Heng builds a seismoscope: a bronze vessel that dropped a ball into one of eight dragon mouths to show the direction of a distant earthquake.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The wheelbarrow, the crank handle and the stern-mounted rudder are all first attested in Han China.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Taichu calendar reform sets the civil year, with its intercalary months, on the footing that Chinese calendars follow in principle to this day.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art: systems of linear equations solved by a method equivalent to Gaussian elimination, rules for negative numbers, and an approximation of pi.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Zhang Heng's water-driven armillary sphere turns with the heavens, and he catalogues about 2,500 stars.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Du Shi harnesses a water wheel to the bellows of a blast furnace. Cast iron becomes cheap enough for ploughshares and hoes.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Brine wells drilled hundreds of meters deep with bamboo derricks in Sichuan, and natural gas piped through bamboo to boil the brine for salt.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Silk woven on multi-shaft treadle looms. Han silks have been found in Roman-era graves at Palmyra in Syria.

passages.title: Arts and letters
passages.text: The tombs at Mawangdui are sealed, preserving silk paintings, a silk map, and the earliest complete copies of the Daodejing.

passages.title: Arts and letters
passages.text: Sima Qian completes the Records of the Grand Historian, 130 chapters covering two thousand years and the model for every later Chinese dynastic history.

passages.title: Arts and letters
passages.text: The fu rhapsodies of Sima Xiangru, the folk songs collected by the Music Bureau, and lacquerware from Sichuan workshops exported across Asia.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Emperor Wu makes the Confucian classics the basis of official learning; the Imperial Academy follows in 124 BCE.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The White Horse Temple at Luoyang, by tradition China's first Buddhist temple, marks the arrival of Buddhism along the Silk Road.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Wang Chong's Lunheng argues that thunder is not the anger of heaven and that the dead have no consciousness.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Zhang Qian sets out for the west. His reports of Ferghana horses, Parthia and India open what is now called the Silk Road.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The Protectorate of the Western Regions is set up in the Tarim Basin, securing the route to Central Asia.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: An embassy claiming to come from the Roman emperor Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus) reaches the Han court by sea, according to the Book of Later Han.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The census counts 57,671,400 people, most of them farming households of about five on small plots of millet, wheat and rice, taxed in grain, cloth and labour.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Chang'an, the Western Han capital, sits inside about 25 km of walls with nine markets, and is one of the two largest cities in the world alongside Rome.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Games of liubo and cuju kickball, and the clay tomb figures of dancers, farmyards and watchtowers that show the Han world in miniature.

Weakened by court factions and the Yellow Turban rebellion of 184, the dynasty ended when Cao Pi accepted the abdication of Emperor Xian in 220. China split into the Three Kingdoms of Wei, Shu and Wu.

passages.text: The Haudenosaunee are a continuing confederacy of nations. The Onondaga Nation's own accounts describe government, food, ceremonies and wampum as living practices connecting community responsibilities with historical memory.

passages.title: Government
passages.text: Clan Mothers select the Hoyane who represent their clans in council. They can remove a leader who fails to represent the clan, after warnings.

passages.title: Technology and memory
passages.text: Wampum makers cut, round, sand and drill shell beads. Woven strings and belts support the remembrance of agreements and their histories.

passages.title: Diplomacy
passages.text: Wampum strings can carry invitations to council meetings. They also identify leadership titles and give weight to a speaker's words.

passages.title: Food and daily life
passages.text: Corn, beans and squash are the Three Sisters. Onondaga food traditions also include fishing, hunting, gathering and sharing food within the community.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Thanksgiving Address opens gatherings by acknowledging people, the natural world and their interdependence. Speakers express it in their own words.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Clan Mothers help sustain ceremonies and teach younger generations. These are present-day responsibilities, not customs of a vanished society.

passages.text: Tawantinsuyu joined diverse Andean regions through roads, administration and local labor. Its infrastructure drew on earlier Andean traditions and adapted construction to mountains, valleys and coastal environments.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Road builders used bridges, stairs, paving and drainage suited to different terrain. The network linked centers of production, government and worship.

passages.title: Food and farming
passages.text: Communities built and maintained terraces that created level planting areas while resisting erosion. Water conduits also protected roads from damaging runoff.

passages.title: Water engineering
passages.text: Stone channels and storage facilities managed rainfall and snowmelt for resources shared among families.

passages.title: Storage
passages.text: Colcas were storehouses whose siting and construction kept supplies cool and dry. Their contents included potatoes, maize, quinoa, clothing and tools.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The road system moved goods including textiles, feathers, food and shell. It incorporated earlier routes and knowledge from Andean communities.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Andean languages and traditions continued under Spanish rule. Weavers combined established textile techniques and designs with new imagery.
Pizarro captured Atahualpa in 1532 and had him killed in 1533. Spanish conquest dismantled imperial government, while Andean peoples continued and adapted their traditions.

passages.text: Kerma was the capital of a Nubian kingdom on the Nile in present-day Sudan. Its prosperity rested on herding, cultivation and exchange between African interiors and Egypt. This page follows the kingdom, its earlier background and what archaeology reveals about its people.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Excavators mapped houses with courtyards containing kitchens and grain silos. These remains show how households organized cooking and storage around shared outdoor space.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Temple workshops and storerooms clustered around the Western Deffufa. A palace contained a large circular building interpreted as a royal audience hall, revealing distinct religious and political spaces.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: At Middle Kerma grave 253, researchers recorded 4,899 cattle skulls. They interpret the association between large tombs and numerous skulls as a display of the deceased person's wealth and power.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Some cattle horns had been deliberately reshaped; cut marks and altered growth preserve evidence of the practice. Researchers suggest specially valued animals were distinguished this way, while warning against copying modern herders' beliefs directly onto ancient Kerma.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: Kerma potters shaped exceptionally thin cups by hand, then polished their red surfaces. Controlled firing produced black rims and interiors, evidence of skilled handling of both clay and the firing atmosphere.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: A tulip-shaped beaker in Manchester Museum was excavated at Kerma in 1913. Its smooth, shining finish was made by burnishing the clay before firing; the form was achieved without a potter's wheel.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: Cattle also appeared in small figurines found in the city and in paintings in a funerary chapel. Their presence in art as well as graves suggests a significance extending beyond food and exchange.

passages.title: Daily life and food
passages.text: Animal bones from the capital show that domestic livestock supplied most of the meat evidence. Cattle, sheep and goats dominated; the researchers observed a later increase in sheep and goats relative to cattle.

passages.title: Daily life and food
passages.text: Fine beakers existed alongside heavier storage jars, sometimes stamped around the rim. Stone implements remained in use beside metal technology, preserving evidence of practical choices in everyday tools.

passages.title: Burial, belief and social rank
passages.text: Graves preserve wooden beds, personal ornaments, sandals and containers for oils or ointments. Larger, richer tombs show growing inequality; some also contained accompanying people interpreted as victims of funerary killing.

passages.title: Trade and cultural connections
passages.text: A Kerma-style beaker now at the Metropolitan Museum was excavated at Abydos in Egypt. Such finds demonstrate connections across the Nile Valley, but the museum cautions that pottery alone cannot establish whether the people buried with it were Nubian traders.

passages.title: What continued after conquest
passages.text: Survey finds include Egyptian pottery together with Nubian pottery. Stuart Tyson Smith interprets the settlement pattern as evidence that some local elites retained cultural and political latitude under Egyptian rule; conquest did not erase Nubian society.

passages.title: What remains uncertain
passages.text: The relationship between the earlier Pre-Kerma settlement and the royal city is not fully demonstrated. Excavated buildings and objects reveal much, but their locations do not establish precise kingdom borders.

Egyptian New Kingdom campaigns ended Kerma's independence. The excavation mission places the capital's destruction around 1450 BCE, after a longer conquest associated with Thutmose I and Thutmose III; this is an approximate endpoint, not a known single day of collapse.

passages.text: The Kuba kingdom brought together several principalities in Central Africa. Royal and aristocratic patronage encouraged inventive textiles, carved vessels and images through which rank and historical memory became visible.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Kuba makers wove raffia palm fibers into cloth. Women joined, dyed and embellished panels with embroidery and applique.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cutting embroidered raffia threads created a dense pile surface. Some panels were displayed as prestige objects and used as currency rather than worn.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Multiple cloth panels formed wrappers whose gathered edges moved with the wearer. Dress combined bodily movement with elaborate surface design.

passages.title: Historical memory
passages.text: Ndop sculptures memorialized rulers through idealized seated figures and identifying symbols. A strategy board identifies Shyaam aMbul aNgoong.

passages.title: Knowledge
passages.text: Kuba chronologies preserve references to a solar eclipse and Halley's comet, giving historians points for comparison with independently dated celestial events.

passages.text: Kush was an African kingdom of the Middle Nile whose centers included Napata and Meroe. Its rulers and craftspeople developed distinctive monuments while exchanging ideas with neighboring societies. The royal city, religious settlements and industrial remains show a civilization extending well beyond its famous pyramids.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Iron-working remains and ceramic production areas at Meroe document skilled manufacture. They establish local production, not a claim that Kush invented iron smelting.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Reservoirs helped support settlements away from the Nile. Their remains are evidence for both engineering and the environmental conditions in which people lived.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Steep-sided pyramids, decorated funerary chapels and painted burial chambers gave Kushite royal commemoration a distinctive appearance.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Architecture at Meroe, Naqa and Musawwarat combined Kushite forms with elements associated with Egypt, Greece and Rome.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Gebel Barkal was a sacred landscape. Temples at its foot connected royal authority with the worship of Amun.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Meroitic political order ended in late antiquity, but burial traditions continued afterward. A kingdom's disappearance should not be read as the disappearance of its people.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Gold and salt served long-distance commerce; cowrie shells also entered local exchange during the fourteenth century.

passages.title: Trade and exchange

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Mande jeliw transmit historical epics through skilled performance. Musical accompaniment helps structure and pace narratives.

passages.text: Maori society comprises distinct iwi and hapu with their own histories and authority. This card introduces shared themes while preserving those differences. The imported map interval is not an extinction date: Maori communities, language and cultural institutions continue.

passages.title: Agriculture
passages.text: Growers adapted horticulture to a cooler climate, using techniques including stone walls and warmed soils to cultivate kumara. Practices varied with local environments.

passages.title: Technology and exchange
passages.text: Pounamu and obsidian supplied tool materials; harakeke supplied fibre. Gift exchange helped move valued materials among communities.

passages.title: Ideas and governance
passages.text: Local groups exercised their own authority. Genealogy connected individuals to wider communities, while tapu and mana shaped relationships with people and natural resources.

passages.title: Science and seasons
passages.text: For many iwi, the midwinter appearance of Matariki marked the new year. Observances differ among iwi and include remembering the dead and sharing the harvest.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Carving, weaving and language revitalisation continued through the twentieth century. Maori communities developed language nests, broadcasting and new work in music, film and art.

passages.text: Maya history encompasses distinct societies and city-states. Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque and Copan supported royal courts with specialized artists; their political histories should be explored individually rather than compressed into one Maya empire.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Some court artists signed their work. The sculptor Chakalte' left his name on a relief showing Shield Jaguar IV receiving tribute.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Stoneworkers carved and polished limestone vessels with tools and abrasives. Shell, bone, jade and fired clay offered other media for intricate objects.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Blue-green jade evoked water, new growth and primordial beings. It became material for offerings, ornaments and royal regalia.

passages.title: Writing and history
passages.text: Tikal's carved and painted inscriptions preserve dynastic history and relationships with other cities. They document particular courts, not a single pan-Maya government.

passages.title: Water and daily life
passages.text: Tikal combined monumental precincts with residential districts and reservoirs known today as aguadas. Its surrounding settlements also supported agricultural production.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: After several Classic-period kingdoms declined, northern centers such as Chichen Itza continued commissioning major artworks. Political collapse in one region did not end Maya history everywhere.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: At Tikal's Corriental reservoir, researchers identified zeolite and coarse quartz in dated sediment layers. They interpret these minerals as evidence of a water filter; its proposed stone supports and woven matting are a reconstruction, not a surviving intact installation.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Water-jar fragments occur throughout Corriental's excavated sediment sequence, linking the reservoir to everyday water collection. The filter evidence comes from this particular reservoir, not from every Maya city.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: At Copan, exposed layers of the Acropolis preserve earlier plaza floors and covered water outlets beneath later construction. These buried surfaces reveal repeated rebuilding of the city rather than a monument created in a single episode.

Maya societies did not share one fall date or one conqueror. UNESCO places Copan's abandonment in the early tenth century, while northern centers continued major artistic production after many Classic courts declined; a local city's decline cannot stand for the end of all Maya societies. Maya communities continue today, with living languages and cultural traditions.

passages.text: Mercia was a kingdom in central England. Large earthworks and the Staffordshire Hoard offer different views of its region: organized construction and highly skilled early medieval metalwork.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Offa's Dyke used a bank and ditch to mark a frontier. English Heritage dates its construction probably to the 780s.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Staffordshire Hoard fragments include intricate gold and garnet decoration. Their designs have connections across several European regions.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Many hoard fragments belonged to an elaborate helmet. Modern reconstruction relies on study of the surviving pieces rather than discovery of an intact helmet.

passages.title: Evidence and daily life
passages.text: The hoard reveals elite craftsmanship and equipment. Its burial location alone cannot identify every maker or make it a representative sample of ordinary Mercian households.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: Scholars from Mercia contributed to the translations supported by Alfred of Wessex. Learned activity crossed the boundaries between neighboring kingdoms.

passages.text: The Marinids made Fez a royal capital and sponsored an urban culture of learning, worship, commerce and craftsmanship. Their new town stood beside the older medina, creating a capital with complementary royal and civic spaces.

passages.title: Technology and towns
passages.text: Fez Jedid was founded in 1276 beside Fez el-Bali. It included the palace, fortifications, military headquarters and residential districts.

passages.title: Learning and beliefs
passages.text: Madrasas and mosques are among the principal monuments associated with the city's Marinid flourishing in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.

passages.title: Daily life and trade
passages.text: Fondouks, houses and fountains belonged to the capital's urban fabric alongside royal and religious buildings.

passages.title: Arts and legacy
passages.text: Fez's architecture brought local skills into conversation with influences from Andalusia and other African and eastern centers. Its craft traditions continued beyond any one dynasty.

passages.text: Minoan is the modern name for Bronze Age Cretan culture, with several palatial centers rather than one securely documented island-wide kingdom. Its crafts, exchange networks and administrative writing linked Crete to the wider Mediterranean.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Palaces at Knossos, Phaistos, Mallia and Zakros grouped rooms around central courts. Lighting, ventilation and sanitary facilities formed part of their design.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: Cretan hieroglyphic writing and Linear A appear on administrative tablets and ritual objects. Palace record keeping helped organize economic activity.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wall paintings show rituals and the natural world. Jewelers worked with filigree and granulation, while engravers carved seal stones.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: A small agate gem in the Met depicts a griffin and is dated approximately 1450 to 1400 BCE. Objects preserve artistic continuity beyond a single palace destruction.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Crete exported timber, textiles, food and luxury crafts, while importing metals and other raw materials.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Widespread destruction around 1450 BCE accompanied growing Mycenaean influence. Linear B administration and mixed pottery styles followed; neither the destruction nor cultural change has a securely identified single cause.

passages.text: Moche societies flourished along Peru's northern coastal valleys during the first through eighth centuries CE. Their ceramics preserve an unusually rich visual record of people, animals, plants and ritual activity.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Potters used molds to produce standardized vessel shapes while varying their painted and sculpted decoration.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Many vessels combine red and cream slip painting with modeled figures. Complex scenes could cover the surface of a stirrup-spout bottle.

passages.title: Portraiture
passages.text: Portrait bottles may depict recognizable individuals. Scholars debate how their social identities related to the vessels' eventual placement in burials.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Fine decorated pottery also occurs in residential compounds. Wear, repairs and excavated household contexts show that many vessels served the living before burial.

passages.title: Food and gatherings
passages.text: Decorated vessels participated in household rituals and feasts, including the sharing of food and corn beer.

passages.title: How we know
passages.text: Images include crops, animals, healers and supernatural beings. They are a visual source, but an image alone cannot tell us every detail of the activity it depicts.

passages.text: In the early twentieth century, Dutch engineers and designers experimented with ways to manage water and domestic space. This chapter pairs a steam pumping station with an adaptable family home.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Wouda pumping station opened at Lemmer in 1920 to help prevent flooding in low-lying Friesland, using steam power to move water.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Wouda installation integrated a boiler house, chimney, fuel storage, drainage canal and sluices. Water management required an entire connected system.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Truus Schroder-Schrader commissioned the house designed by Gerrit Rietveld in Utrecht in 1924. Its design expressed ideas associated with De Stijl.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The Schroder House used a flexible internal arrangement so rooms could change with their functions. Furniture and interior space were treated as parts of one design.

passages.text: Northumbria joined the regions of Bernicia and Deira. Its royal centers and monasteries supported learning, manuscript production and religious networks reaching beyond northern Britain.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: King Oswald invited Aidan from Iona to establish a monastery at Lindisfarne in 635. Royal support placed the foundation near the kingdom's political center.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Lindisfarne Gospels were made approximately 710 to 725. They are evidence of the monastery's role as a center of Christian learning and book production.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Pilgrims came to Cuthbert's shrine, while patrons gave land, money and precious objects. Religious devotion helped support the monastery's economy.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: Runic name stones commemorate Anglo-Saxon inhabitants of Lindisfarne, preserving writing outside the pages of books.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: The monastic community moved inland during Viking-era disruption, carrying treasures and relics. Carved stones show that Christian burial continued on Lindisfarne after the monks left.

passages.text: Numidian society belongs to North Africa's indigenous history and its wider Mediterranean connections. Thugga, now Dougga, offers evidence for urban life under Numidian kings and for its transformation under Roman rule. The spectacular Roman monuments there are later additions to an older town.

passages.title: Technology and towns
passages.text: At Thugga, Roman construction was fitted into a largely Numidian street pattern. Urban continuity survived the change of political authority.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: Libyan, Punic and bilingual inscriptions help reconstruct Numidian social and municipal life. Their study also contributed to deciphering Libyan writing.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Libyco-Punic mausoleum preserves an important pre-Roman monumental tradition, although its modern reconstruction complicates interpretation of the standing structure.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Under Rome, an indigenous community and a legally distinct group of Roman citizens coexisted at Thugga. Cultural change did not require the town's earlier inhabitants to vanish.

passages.text: Olmec names a group of early Mesoamerican societies, especially those of Mexico's Gulf Coast. Their monumental building projects and stoneworking joined local farming communities to far-reaching networks of materials and artistic ideas.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: At San Lorenzo, communities cooperated to build large earthen platforms and mounds. These were shared construction projects beyond the needs of individual households.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Artists worked both enormous volcanic-stone sculptures and small, finely finished jade objects. Those materials could travel from distant sources.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Maize farming helped sustain communities in Gulf Coast river valleys, although many details of San Lorenzo's households remain under investigation.

passages.title: Games
passages.text: Rubber balls recovered at El Manati provide early evidence for the place of ballgames in Olmec life.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: La Venta's carvings connect rulers with watery environments and agricultural fertility. Their imagery draws on the surrounding landscape.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: La Venta flourished especially between 1000 and 500 BCE and was apparently abandoned by 400 BCE. That local sequence does not establish one universal fall for all Olmec societies.

passages.text: The Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy used Ravenna as a royal center. Its surviving buildings and personal ornaments show both distinctive traditions and close engagement with the Roman world.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Theodoric's mausoleum used large blocks of Istrian stone arranged around a central space.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Sant'Apollinare Nuovo began as Theodoric's palace chapel. Its mosaics combined Roman traditions with eastern Mediterranean influence.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Arian Baptistery preserves imagery expressing the court's Christian faith. The Archbishop's Chapel represents a different Christian community in the same city.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: In wider Ostrogothic dress, pairs of shoulder brooches secured women's long garments. Decorated belts, necklaces and other jewelry completed the ensemble.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A surviving brooch attributed to wider Ostrogothic material culture was cast in silver, with silver covering its copper-alloy pin. It combined practical fastening and ornament; the record does not establish manufacture in Italy.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Ravenna passed from Ostrogothic to Byzantine rule. Buildings surviving together today belong to different patrons and periods; San Vitale's Justinianic decoration should not be credited to Theodoric.

passages.text: This chapter follows Renaissance planning and learning in Poland-Lithuania. Zamosc offers a local view of how architectural ideas, commerce and education could meet in one deliberately planned town.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Union of Lublin joined the Polish Crown and Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the Commonwealth under one monarch in 1569.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the late sixteenth century, Bernardo Morando designed Zamosc using Italian Renaissance ideas of an ideal city, adapted to Central European architectural traditions.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Zamosc was conceived as a trading centre on a route connecting western and northern Europe with the Black Sea. Arcaded merchants' houses enclosed its main market square.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Founder Jan Zamoyski established the Zamosc Academy. The planned town combined education with residential, commercial and civic functions.

passages.text: This chapter follows Portuguese architecture and learning from the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries, through Lisbon's Belem complex and Coimbra's colleges, laboratories and printing facilities.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: In sixteenth-century Belem, the Hieronymites monastery combined richly carved Manueline decoration with spaces for worship, meals, study and communal life.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Belem tower incorporated ribbed cupolas inspired by Islamic architecture. Its design records artistic exchange across cultural boundaries.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Coimbra University has occupied the Royal Palace of Alcacova since 1537 and expanded through a network of colleges.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: In the eighteenth century, Coimbra added chemistry and other laboratories, a botanical garden and a university press. These facilities linked teaching, experimentation and the circulation of books.

passages.text: This chapter follows the designed landscapes and museum ambitions associated with Prussia in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. It focuses on architects, craftspeople and the institutions that organized their work.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Frederick II commissioned Sanssouci between 1745 and 1747. The palace later hosted the French writer Voltaire.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, Potsdam's parks combined architecture with landscape gardening. Builders, painters, sculptors and gardeners contributed to the ensemble.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: During the nineteenth century, Peter Joseph Lenne planned changes to the Havel landscape around Potsdam. Designed parkland linked water, buildings and views.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Museum Island project in Berlin began in the nineteenth century. It treated museum architecture and the display of art and archaeology as a connected public undertaking.

passages.text: Pueblo societies comprise distinct communities and histories. Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde preserve ancestral building and farming landscapes; Taos Pueblo is a living community with its own traditions and government.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: At Chaco, builders planned multistory Great Houses whose construction could span generations. Their masonry and shared layouts mark a regional architectural tradition.

passages.title: Science and landscape
passages.text: Many Chaco structures were oriented toward solar, lunar or cardinal directions. Their placement linked buildings to a meaningful surrounding landscape.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Mesa Verde preserves farming terraces, check dams, reservoirs and ditches as well as houses. These remains document the engineering of everyday subsistence.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Roads connected Chaco Great Houses across the region. Some major buildings may have hosted periodic ceremonies and exchange rather than dense permanent populations.

passages.title: Living architecture
passages.text: At Taos, families maintain adobe homes by renewing earthen plaster. Taos describes that work as an ongoing connection between ancestors and the present.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Changes in ancestral settlements did not end Pueblo life. Mesa Verde remains a living connection to present-day Pueblo peoples, and Taos continues as a sovereign community.

passages.text: For four centuries one government ruled every shore of the Mediterranean, from the Atlantic to the Euphrates and from Hadrian's Wall to the first cataract of the Nile. Rome invented little that was wholly new and perfected almost everything it borrowed: Greek architecture became concrete vaults, Etruscan drains became aqueducts, and a city-state's customs became a body of law that most of Europe still lives under. Its language, Latin, is the parent of Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian and Romanian.

passages.title: Inventions and building
passages.text: Roman concrete, opus caementicium, mixed with volcanic ash so that it set even under water. The harbour moles built with it at Caesarea and Portus still stand.

passages.title: Inventions and building
passages.text: Vitruvius completes De architectura, ten books on building, water, machines and city planning that guided Renaissance architects fifteen centuries later.

passages.title: Inventions and building
passages.text: The Colosseum opens: about 50,000 seats, a retractable awning, and eighty entrances so the whole crowd could leave in minutes.

passages.title: Inventions and building
passages.text: The Pantheon's concrete dome, 43.3 meters across, is completed under Hadrian. It is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Pliny the Elder publishes the Natural History, thirty-seven books that try to gather everything then known about the natural world.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Ptolemy, working in Alexandria, writes the Almagest, the geocentric model of the heavens that stood for 1,400 years, and a Geography that placed the known world on a grid of coordinates.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Galen arrives in Rome. His dissections of animals describe the nerves, the heart and the pulse, and his anatomy is taught in Europe until the sixteenth century.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Aqueducts: eleven serve the city of Rome by 226 CE, feeding public fountains, baths and a sewer system, the Cloaca Maxima, that still drains the Forum.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Roads: about 80,000 km of paved highway across the empire by the second century, cambered for drainage, with milestones and way stations a day's ride apart.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The codex, pages bound at the spine, begins to replace the scroll; by the fourth century it is the normal form of the book.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The mills at Barbegal near Arles: sixteen water wheels in two descending rows, grinding grain for a whole town.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Virgil dies leaving the Aeneid unfinished. Augustus orders it published against the poet's wishes, and it becomes Rome's national epic.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Ovid completes the Metamorphoses, the retelling of Greek and Roman myth that fed European painting and poetry for two thousand years.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Trajan's Column: a 30-meter spiral of carved relief telling the story of the Dacian wars in 155 scenes.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Portrait sculpture that shows the sitter warts and all, mosaic floors from Britain to Syria, and the wall paintings of Pompeii, sealed by Vesuvius in 79 CE.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Roman law: the praetors' edicts and the jurists' commentaries, later gathered under Justinian, are the root of the civil law systems of continental Europe and Latin America.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Seneca, Stoic philosopher and tutor to Nero, is ordered to kill himself, leaving the Letters to Lucilius. Stoicism was the working philosophy of the Roman elite.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Constantine's Edict of Milan grants freedom of worship. Christianity, persecuted a decade earlier, becomes the religion of the emperors.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Edict of Thessalonica makes Nicene Christianity the state religion.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Public baths in every town, with hot and cold rooms, exercise yards and libraries. Entry cost a quadrans, the smallest coin.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: A market the size of the Mediterranean: Spanish olive oil, Egyptian grain, Gaulish wine and Indian pepper moved in amphorae. Monte Testaccio in Rome is a hill made of an estimated 53 million broken oil jars.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Insulae, apartment blocks of five or more storeys, housed most of Rome's roughly one million people, the largest city in the world until the nineteenth century.

On the death of Theodosius I in 395 the empire was divided between his sons Arcadius and Honorius and never reunited. The Western half fell in 476; the Eastern half, which we call Byzantine, lasted until 1453.

passages.text: Songhai's wealth linked Gao and the Niger region to trans-Saharan commerce. Its surviving monuments make construction, religious practice and shared maintenance visible alongside the better-known history of its rulers.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: At Gao, the Tomb of Askia combines an earthen pyramidal tower with mosque buildings, a cemetery and an assembly space.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Projecting wooden supports form permanent scaffolding. Renewing rain-eroded plaster is part of the building's continuing life.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: During the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, Timbuktu was a center of Islamic learning and manuscript exchange.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Timbuktu's market brought together manuscripts, salt, gold, cattle and grain. Scholarship existed within a busy commercial city.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The mosques of Djingareyber, Sankore and Sidi Yahia preserve an earthen architectural tradition shaped by successive restorations.

passages.text: Architecture and painting show different sides of Spain's sixteenth- and seventeenth-century culture: a royal monastery organized around worship and learning, and pictures shaped by observation and international exchange.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Philip II founded El Escorial in 1563. Juan Bautista de Toledo designed the complex, and Juan de Herrera completed the work after Toledo's death.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: El Escorial combined a monastery, church, palace, school, seminary and royal library around courtyards. Religious life, royal authority and study occupied one complex.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Early in his seventeenth-century career, Velazquez painted kitchen scenes known as bodegones and studied figures directly from life.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Velazquez became painter to Philip IV in 1623. Later at Madrid, Venetian paintings and contact with Rubens helped shape his art.

passages.text: Early-modern Sweden supported both industrial communities and elaborate court art. Falun's copper landscape and Drottningholm's theatre reveal very different kinds of skilled work.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the seventeenth century, Falun copper production helped make Sweden a major European metal producer. Mining shaped the surrounding economy and settlement landscape.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Falun's seventeenth-century planned town and mining settlements preserve evidence of workers' housing as well as production facilities. Industrial history includes the communities around the mine.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Drottningholm's eighteenth-century theatre used machinery that could change scenery while the curtain stayed up. Stage sets and working mechanisms survive.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Drottningholm's Chinese Pavilion reflects eighteenth-century European engagement with Asian design. Nearby Canton Village included manufacturing buildings and court living quarters.

passages.text: Teotihuacan was a major urban center in central Mexico. Its public monuments, apartment compounds and specialized arts connected a large city with other Mesoamerican communities through exchange and influence.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The urban layout incorporated the San Juan River, whose course was altered to cross the Avenue of the Dead.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Builders used talud-tablero profiles, combining sloping and upright wall sections, in civil and religious architecture.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Apartment compounds grouped connected rooms around open courtyards. They provided durable shared housing for much of the city's population.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Murals decorated many buildings, especially residential compounds. Artists also made mold-pressed ceramics and geometric stone faces.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Imported craft goods included worked obsidian and Thin Orange pottery. Stackable bowls made long-distance transport more practical.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: The Met's updated account places burning in the monumental core around 550 CE and marked population decline after 600. The people responsible are unidentified.

passages.text: Venice joined lagoon engineering to a far-reaching artistic culture. This chapter follows the city and its painters during the Renaissance; it does not yet cover the republic's entire history.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: During the republic, canals connected settlements consolidated from lagoon islands. Hydraulic and architectural work continually reshaped the relationship between the city and its surrounding water.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: In sixteenth-century Venice, Titian, Veronese and Tintoretto developed influential approaches to painting. Their work later shaped artists including Rubens and Velazquez.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: After moving from Verona in the 1550s, Veronese found both civic and church commissions in Venice. Artistic employment crossed religious and governmental settings.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The lagoon included fishing settlements and artisan communities such as Murano. Venice's palaces were part of a larger landscape of work and settlement.

passages.text: Wessex was a kingdom in southern England. Under Alfred, royal support for reading and translation linked learned texts with the skilled production of books and precious objects.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: Alfred commissioned translations of religious works from Latin into Old English. Copies circulated within his kingdom.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Some books were accompanied by reading pointers called aestels. The Alfred Jewel may have formed the head of one, but its function remains an interpretation.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The jewel combines gold, colored cloisonne enamel and rock crystal. A figure appears beneath the crystal, and an animal-like head forms the base.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: An inscription names Alfred as the person who ordered the object made. The museum dates it to his reign, 871 to 899.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The figure beneath the crystal may personify sight, fitting a possible reading aid. The museum presents this identification as uncertain.

passages.title: Ideas and institutions
passages.text: Alfred's law code drew on earlier West Saxon, Mercian and Kentish rules. His government also supported fortified market settlements, connecting defense with economic activity.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Wessex became the base from which Alfred's successors expanded royal power across England. This was a process of political consolidation, not the disappearance of West Saxon people.

passages.text: Yolngu peoples maintain distinct clan identities in Arnhem Land. Country, law, food, ceremony and art remain connected, while institutions at Yirrkala carry knowledge through contemporary media.

passages.title: Worldview and institutions
passages.text: Dhuwa and Yirritja are complementary moieties connecting people, places and other living beings. In Miwatj, art and ceremony express relationships to fresh and saltwater Country.

passages.title: Food and seasons
passages.text: Seasonal food gathering draws on both land and sea, including yams, fruit, fish and shellfish. Traditional owners connect these practices with law and ceremony.

passages.title: Art and diplomacy
passages.text: Artists framed the Yirrkala petitions with clan designs in ochre, charcoal and pipeclay. These designs expressed relationships to land alongside text in English and Yolngu Matha.

passages.title: Political history
passages.text: Yolngu presented bark petitions to the Australian Parliament in 1963 in response to mining plans made without adequate consultation. They understood the documents as a diplomatic offering between equal powers.

passages.title: Digital knowledge
passages.text: The Mulka Project combines a recording studio, production house, learning centre and cultural archive under Yolngu law and elder leadership. It trains community members and returns audiovisual records to communities.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: A bark petition formerly held privately was formally returned to Yolngu at Yirrkala in 2023. Its return forms part of continuing cultural custody.

passages.text: Monte Alban was an important Zapotec capital in the Oaxaca Valley. Its history of urban planning, water management and carved inscriptions is one part of the much wider history of Zapotec societies.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders reshaped hillsides with terraces, dams and conduits. Water management and the creation of level spaces were integrated into urban development.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Temples and platforms framed a long ceremonial esplanade. Open spaces were as important to the layout as the buildings themselves.

passages.title: Writing and arts
passages.text: Carved reliefs with hieroglyphic inscriptions survive alongside tombs and temples, giving evidence of visual art and record making.

passages.title: Public life
passages.text: The ceremonial center included a ball court. Its built spaces supported activities beyond the palaces and burial places of elites.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Monte Alban maintained relations with Teotihuacan. Those contacts connect Oaxaca's history to other contemporary Mesoamerican centers.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: UNESCO dates Monte Alban's long florescence from about 500 BCE to 850 CE, followed by decline. This is the trajectory of a city, not an extinction date for Zapotec peoples.
